The malicious force of will automating each assemblage of wood and flesh before her – the gestalt total of occult programming driving this useless werewolf machine – draws the vines in her mind upwards, into the darkness where she senses what used to be a pile of furry meat emerge as a living creature just long enough to recognize that it’s falling before hitting the grinders below. “Where the hell are we?” Amitha whispers. “Never seen this sub-basement before.” Egret’s voice is tighter than usual. Submind Tenchu bursts from her mouth in a splash of blood. “It belonged to my predecessor.” Amitha recoils and slips off the corpse pile, landing flat on her back. The wormtongue retreats long enough for Egret to stumble down the flesh hill and extend a hand to Amitha with the fluidity of a damaged puppet. “Good news!” she says. “We’ve re-established contact with the boss. ” “Erin,” echoes a voice behind them. Amitha whirls to see a horde of mangled bodies dragging themselves out of the machine, down from the pile, into the control room. Clotted blood dribble from exposed innards. Shards of glass and chunks of wood protrude from mashed torsos and shattered limbs. As if through one mouth, each decaying creature utters, “Kill me.”   Tenchu’s mouth protrudes just over Egret’s lips. “This is Overseer Six speaking,” it says. “This amateurish construction deserves no other moniker than Briar. I want him alive. Curious to know how he bypassed my safety countermeasures.” Tenchu speaks in one of the Overseer’s crueler voices. “I //ate// them alive.” Briar’s voice forces its way through multiple cadaverous throats at once, each clogged by bone and blood. “Kill me, Erin,” the werewolf corpses say in unison. “We deserve it.” A teeth-grinding rattle emerges at the tail end of their words. “Yes, you do,”says Six as Egret faces the horde. A sigh escapes from Egret’s lips that makes Amitha’s hair stand on end. Some invisible force riding the sigh batters each werewolf in turn. They stumble and then crumple as their skeletons fall out through their backs. Human skeletons. From wolf skins. “Submind Tenchu – Overseer,” Amitha chokes out. “What the hell is this thing? Why is it in your basement?” The wormtongue winds around Egret’s shoulder to look at her. How does it do that without eyes? “You recall your participation in SATURNINE CALENDAR PACIFICATION?” it says in one of the Overseer’s cruel voices. “These are the remains of a similar stellar entity. My predecessor contained it… and then overstepped the bounds of his competence. I constructed this machine to contain him.” “We… constructed it,” the wolfskins wheeze. “Are you so afraid of your… protege you would lie to her?” “Kindly shut up,” Six says.  “I was young when we built this. You were not.” “We killed it together, Erin. Amitha. I have had the… privilege of observing –” “Kindly shut up,” Six repeats. There’s a sour taste in the air. Blood in Amitha’s ears. In her eyes. Her lips have sealed themselves. The skins don’t have mouths anymore. “Egret,” says Tenchu, “I’ve allowed you full knowledge of this facility’s layout and systems. It will be scrubbed once you leave. Amitha? Have Egret show you where the killswitch is and call a cleanup team once you’re done. I’d handle this myself but Three’s caused yet another budget crisis I’ve been tasked with solving. There may be some aggressive internal reorganization and headcount reduction to divine. I have full faith in your ability to deal with this issue in my stead.” The wormtongue vanishes back into Egret’s mouth with a horrifying slurp. Amitha fights back a wave of nausea and looks at the re-obliterated bodies. Bad idea. Thick chunks of black clot dribble out from each discarded skin, trailing towards the pile of bones that belonged to them. The amoebic mass slides under the pile and recedes like a tide, dragging its owners’ skeletons back into place. Amitha loses the fight and vomits onto the floor – mostly coffee. By the time she’s finished wiping her mouth, the standing skin-sacks are on the move again. “Man.” Egret bares her teeth at the shambling bags of skin and bone. “Have the dignity to stay down.” “Silence, dog,” comes a voice out of the walls. “I taught your master how to make you.” “We don’t take orders from you,” Egret snarls, ready to lunge if needed. “Ami. C’mon. We’ve got work to —” Amitha watches in horror as her bodyguard disappears under a waterfall of werewolf bodies. She backs away, waiting for Egret to extract herself, but the pile on top of her grows even as its shattered components burst forth from its lumpen sides to join the advancing pack. “Let me share my wisdom,” say the broken bodies behind her. Amitha turns to find shattered wolf corpses in every direction. “It would be child’s play to kill you. That would not change the circumstances of my hell.” “What could you possibly teach me that the boss couldn’t?” Amitha is barely listening. Most of her is frantically throwing open doors throughout her mathematical palace, chasing down the pseudo-Riemannian infestation of vines she set loose. Looking for the brutest-force solution to her predicament. There’s going to be a lot of pruning if she survives. Emphasis on //if//. “Who gave Erin the seed variables she passed to you? Whose home do you think this was? I sought to learn the secrets of the universe so I might pass them on to the next generation. She hoards it to remake them in her image. What would Erin gain by removing her leverage over you? In raising you from tool to //equal//?” Impossible for her not to hear that. “At least entertain my offer,” says the machine. “I mastered the connections between ritual and biological process before she was born. I recruited her. I trained her. I loved her. She repaid me with this. I have nothing left to lose and everything to gain.” “I just need to find the killswitch,” Amitha says, edging towards the stairs. The world is slowing to a crawl, though from enhanced perception or mathematical poisoning she’s not yet sure. “You want to die. I want you dead. The boss will solve both our problems with the flip of a switch.” “When Erin becomes bored enough she will switch me back //on//. I have relived my own beheading a million times over and will relive it a million more. How many of your peers has your Overseer dispatched through me? How many death sentences can I serve? My knowledge is my penance. My instruction will be my revenge.” A series of cuts emerge in the pyramid, outlining a square hole through a section of furry limbs scrabbling for purchase. Dismembered claws and paws burst from the hole like bloody streamers, followed by a head and arm holding a boxcutter knife. Egret digs the blade into something – an eye, a head, a chest, she can’t tell, all that matters is it's solid enough for purchase to pull herself out of the pile, down the hill of corpses, and begin to stand. She immediately finds herself buried up to the neck in another pile of bodies, clawing, gnawing, growling. Amitha looks away but still hears the crunch of shattered vertebrae. “I sense your loyalties, beast. I agree with your assessment of Ahmadi’s protege,” the walls say. “Let me help you. Both of you. End my suffering, master of ceremonies.” “I’m not allowed to listen to you,” Egret says. “Can you hurry up and finish me off? Boss’ll make it hurt even more if you keep her waiting.” “As you wish.” Amitha watches the pile eat Egret alive until all that remains is a head staring blankly back at her. “The choice is simple,” the wolves say with impatient finality. “Learn from me. Or die like your bodyguard and wait for Erin to drag you back from hell. Assuming she still finds you of use.” “You think she hasn’t done it before?” Amitha squints and pokes the werewolf in front of her. It blinks with empty sockets. Everything is in slow motion. “She’s pulled me back personally on the operating table. There are loyalty oaths where half my glands used to be. I’ve got a little bastard like you instead of a hypothalamus. It’s shaped like a leech, spontaneously generated by the Overseer and sustained by my biochemistry.” Amitha sounds impressed despite herself. “It’s the most amazing feat of biomagical engineering I’ve ever seen. I can’t imagine what it could do if I betrayed her. Show me something more impressive than that, fleabag. Show me something my //boss// would kill for.” A hundred full-mouthed smiles bare themselves across a hundred canid corpses. “Overseer suits me much better, I think.” A loud crunch interrupts them both as Submind Tenchu bursts from Egret’s mouth. Amitha is surprised there was anything left of it. “Ignore him, Archmagus,” it says desperately. “Remember that everything he knows I have surpassed.” “Has she taught you how to surpass me?” Briar asks through a hundred broken mouths. Congealed blood in shattered limbs melt back into oxygenizing molecules fueling the regrowth of shattered bones. A horde of battered bodies reassemble themselves through a method that Amitha comprehends not as but music. The pyramid of corpses reshapes itself into a battalion of werewolves, pinning down the pipe of flesh extending from what remains of Egret with military precision.  “Can you undo this? Has selling your soul to this witch paid dividends?  Have you derived the knowledge needed to topple a corpse a century out of date?” “Amitha…” the wormtongue hisses. Amitha squints at it. “Well, //boss//?” she asks. “Are you going to help me or do I need to look for other options?” How can that damnable thing roll its eyes without having any? A hideous heaving and crunching draws Amitha’s gaze to the bulge spurting through the wormtongue’s three-meter throat. The room holds its collective breath as gasping squelches echo through the chamber. Finally, torturously, Submind Tenchu coughs up a thick, crimson wad of meat before dissolving into a sludge of rainbow-colored proteins. It lands directly before Amitha, who watches the insides of the blob – no, the embryo – divide and develop through its translucent skin. A timelapse of conception and birth in a cold glass womb flashes past in an instant. The newborn beast blinks up at her with Egret’s eyes. An elongated smile of recognition spreads across its face. Exposes fangs. “A troglobite operative?” the useless werewolf machine asks scornfully. “An impressive reconstitution, but hardly enough to deal with me.” “It’s not for you,” the creature says in Egret’s voice. Its four setae-covered claws dig into Amitha’s upper torso, the better to messily devour her. She can’t help but scream. The room falls silent and watches the doctor’s guard dog rip her into chunks that vanish into its gullet. The useless werewolf machine itself slows to process this utter and total betrayal. “You //bitch//!” The declaration is unanimous in its full-throated outrage. The room falls on top of the newborn Egret and messily devours her. ------ + High Treason Under God Phantom itches of rent flesh play along Amitha’s simulated skin, from nape to navel and fingers to feet. She scratches idly at her hands, glare fixed firmly on the Overseer. The mold-colored centipede perched behind the desk does its best to look sheepish, albeit behind a maple-ivory desk like an aircraft carrier afloat in an ocean of Persian carpet. She meets each of its unpleasantly human eyes and sees instantly through the facade. “Is this your mind-space? You never taught me this one.” Amitha screws her face as tightly as she can without shutting her eyes. This may be the only chance she ever gets to be cross with her boss, in a purgatory consisting of whatever is left of her brain tissue. “More specifically, this is an oneiroparasitic incubation chamber. A tool I derived from item number 3199, by which a sufficiently skilled thaumaturge may cannibalize a host to reconstitute their own flesh. I keep one in each member of Red Right Hand.” The grub’s myriad stubby limbs pretend to steeple. God dammit. It’s using the Overseer’s human voice, the lecturing one. Its mandibles chitter silently, making the incongruity of the voice even worse. “I planned to teach you later in your professional development. Before you committed what some would say was an incredibly stupid act of treason.” “That’s not what your archmage calls it,” Amitha says. The mere fact she isn’t in horrific agony means the Overseer doesn’t have time for torture. Means the boss needs her to think for herself. She relishes the capacity for sarcasm. “Indeed,” the grub replies. “You are not incredibly stupid. Stupidly ambitious, perhaps. But. Out of respect for your expertise and –” the grub stares through her, mandibles drooling now at the tiny golem impersonating her hypothalamus “ — commitment to this Foundation, I will interpret your attempted treason as a provocative act of feedback, read between the lines, and acknowledge your necessary criticism.” It leans back. “ You are welcome.” “Boss!” Extra rows of teeth grind behind Amitha’s frustrated scoff. “Stop jerking me around. You fucked this up right and proper by not telling me what I was walking into. Fucked it up further by waiting for me to figure out what I was doing with minimal information. And now you’re being fucked — pardon your bodyguard’s language —  by the consequences of your own actions!” “Do not take that tone with me!” The grub’s upper body lunges forward and pauses over the edge of the massive table.  “Do not pretend you comprehend the consequences of my actions. Nor the prices I pay for them.” “Do not take that tone with me!” Infuriated fangs sprout from Amitha’s mouth, widening and expanding to make room for more fangs, filling both the witch doctor’s jaws and the room itself. Blood starts dripping from the corners of the wall. The grub stops steepling, starts watching as Amitha’s six-clawed hands dig into the desk and lengthen across its surface, like angry giants from a distant shore. This death glare she learned from her mother. “You’re just a fragment of a fragment of a mind I cannot comprehend so you better comprehend how pissed off I am to be cleaning up her mess!” she bellows. “Don’t you dare talk back to //me//, you //worm//! Remind your god that I have willingly sacrifice everything I //can// at the Foundation’s altar. Family, memory, conscience, //flesh//. You tell your fucking boss that I am not just a subordinate, but a collaborator, and to be as effective as possible then I need my Overseer to meet me halfway and collaborate!”   The grub tries to shrink back as the ceiling’s fangs brush across its flesh. Amitha doesn’t dare move for fear of showing weakness. Hot air steams from the centipede’s mandibles and its limbs wriggle in dismay.  “The Overseer was displeased by the interruption,” it grumbles, “//but// offered an apology for dismissing their knowledge of this place on the grounds that they were younger and thus prone to error at the time such as minimizing Briar’s existence, end apology. You have been cleared for all information about this location. Take this opportunity to learn.” Amitha considers it behind a practiced flat stare. “Thank you for the apology. Overseer. Please teach me.” The room bites down on them. — The useless werewolf machine behind the glass was formerly known as Briar Everwood. It strangled the name [[[scp-7660 | out of a would-be assassin]]] during its tenure as O5-6, but lost its past humanity in the process. This is almost certainly the reason its protege, Erin Ahmadi, decided to stage a coup. If only Erin had known that drainage occurred the moment power swapped hands. But the machine once known both as Briar and the Overseer has had decades to stew, complain, and plead with gods it neither believed in nor respected. All it has left is spite, contemplation, and patience. Enough to become the lord of Ahmadi’s Hades. Having spent the last eighty years slowly retaking control of its former citadel, from machinery to security to the rituals designed specifically to incapacitate it, Briar’s machine is ready to seize the final elements needed: doctor Amitha Sanmugasundaram, potential enough to strip Ahmadi of their throne despite the accumulated knowledge to have stripped Briar of its throne. All that remains is to dig through the brain matter being digested in the remains of Ahmadi’s failsafe, the corpse formerly known as Asset Egret. As the archmagus’ flesh is digested by the useless werewolf machine, it grudgingly admits to her skill. Amitha has already learned enough to shield herself behind a labyrinth based on cryptography sophisticated enough to burn out the average quantum supercomputer. Briar, however, is more sophisticated than that. Virtually no time at all elapses before it subsumes and consumes the knowledge protecting Dr. Amitha Sanmugasundaram. Suddenly Briar perceives himself – not as a mass of bodies and tortured flesh in reality, but as a wolf with a man’s face, stuck at the forefront of a painfully white garden of forking paths. Graying chalk lines, the manifestation of mathematical formulae passed down from Briar’s predecessor all the way down to its chosen successor Amitha, trace a path towards the center of her memory palace. Said route is hardly a jaunt in the park; with every step Briar takes, he eliminates a trap meant to instantly flatten the brain matter of a hypothetical psychic trying to infiltrate the good doctor. There is a brand new office room in the deepest bowels of Amitha’s memory garden, identical to Submind Tenchu’s but for one change: Amitha is now the one in the chair. At her command, the split-off chunk of O5-6 grudgingly extends itself through her mind to stymie and irritate the Being known as Briar Everwood. Tenchu lives inside Egret, and Egret lives to obey Amitha. On one dozen screens, Amitha watches the man-wolf pad through her array of traps: dodging oil boiled out of her phobias, crossing vats of stored memetic excrement, and bridging punji pits lined with intrusive thoughts. She doesn’t bother thinking about what remains of Egret. Her newfound knowledge has convinced her that Ahmadi’s killswitch is pointless – this wretched place needs to come down on top of them while she has learned how to survive it. As Briar follows the slightly off-white lines differentiating Ahmadi and Amitha’s mental consciousness; as he derives the electromagnetic frequencies needed to neutralize Sanmugasundaram’s laser grids; struggles to determine the product of primes which its protege borrowed but its protege’s protege managed to factor – he realizes that this is no decaying castle. This is a fortress designed to clamp its jaws around intruders. How does it still function after he clamped his jaws around Amitha? At some point, Briar stumbles across an amphitheater with a single audience member: a colossal, pastel-green stag, a ring of ice behind its head, enraptured by a performance meant for its eyes only. When he tries to pass, the deer instantly turns its face to him and he freezes. Instinctively, he knows he must wait for the performance to end. So he watches as Amitha takes up the role of Fear in a masked farce, hands over a box of cheap sweets to Joy and Apathy, and wields a hammer to labor over stone. He watches her take up the same sickle to castrate a man and euthanize an infant: the former with casual swiftness, the latter with reverent calm. Amitha does not flinch as she practices the blood libel in the name of a God she has sworn to subjugate. As the performance ends, Briar applauds in spite of himself. Then it begins again. And again. And again. The audience remains enraptured. It’s quite the trap, he muses to himself upon escaping. Guilt, contained and weaponized. The wolf and the worm confront each other in the central garden of Amitha Sanmugasundaram’s mind, underneath a rotten tree stuffed with neutralized cognitohazards. “Is this the final trap?” Briar says scornfully. “Who do you think gave you the seed variables to plant this in the first place?” “It is a negotiation," says Tenchu. “You say you wished to train the Archmagus. I say I have been forced to train the Archmagus. We share similar goals.” “The dead Archmagus,” says Briar. “Do you truly believe that?” They stare at each other. “What are the proposed terms?” Briar finally says. “You are consumed by the archmagus Sanmugasundaram,” says Tenchu. “Your mind and body are obliterated. Your knowledge lives on.” Briar considers. “And if I disagree?” Tenchu answers. “You are consumed by the archmagus Sanmugasundaram. Your mind and body are obliterated. Your knowledge lives on.” Briar scoffs as its eyes dilate. “I taught Erin how to craft this palace. I planted this hydra in her mind first. I have made it to the center of Amitha’s garden. What makes you think I cannot possibly consume her?” Tenchu opens its mouth. “Solution Theta-Prime.” Above them, the tree blooms into a fluid dynamics simulation of canid blood coagulation, expressed as protein folds in response to sudden and abrupt full-body trauma and deployed via law of contagion to suffocate any kind of dog within a kilometer radius. The instant Briar looks at it, it realizes how its own route through Amitha’s mind palace – how its path through her brain matter –  forms a sufficient haruspicy circle to obliterate it. All that remained was to trigger it. An industrial line of butchery and horror suddenly and explosively chokes on its own blood. Pipes rupture, bellows burst, pistons seize, and flesh rots exponentially. Gas builds. Fuel leaks. Sparks fly. From basement to spire, Overseer Six’s black-site personal laboratory vanishes in a plume of fire. ------ + Workin' for a Livin' Dr. Amitha Sanmugasundaram, the Archmagus of Overseer Six, has met her Overseer in the flesh only once per decade – until now. For once, Six's factotum remains the same: dark-haired, dark-skinned, severe in expression, hands clasped in front of her, one bare and the other heavy with rings. In place of human eyes burn lights that blind like the Sun. Once upon a time, Amitha would have been forced to look away. She might have stared at the table or the purposely dimmed ceiling bulb or the one-way mirror. In all cases she would have cursed the luck that placed her into an Alpha-1 interrogation room. But she’s learned how to stare back. The werewolf machine taught her after it died. Six blinks first. “My safehouse. My laboratory. My submind. By all means, Archmagus. Explain yourself.” Amitha replies in Submind Tenchu’s voice. “That safehouse was compromised by your predecessor. Your laboratory was, by your own accord, amateurish. Your submind’s intractability hindered my work. It may have gone on to affect yours had I not subjugated it.” Six raises her eyebrows. “And the entity contained in the machine?” “Briar was put into that machine because he was incompetent,” says Amitha. “We are only speaking because I am not. The WOLF is contained. Trapped in an infinite maze.” She taps her head. “I never knew your original name. Erin Ahmadi. I like it.” “Is that a threat?” “It’s a reminder,” Amitha says. “I am not your subordinate. I am your collaborator. Everything I have done, I have done for your vision. For the good of the work. I want to learn! I want to be better for you. Kill me if you find that unacceptable. You’ll find the disruption to your work even  less acceptable.” “You say that as if I am not prepared for such eventualities,” Ahmadi replies. Amitha rolls her eyes. “I was forced to reconstitute myself and your operative from what cooked animal flesh survived the implosion of your safehouse. Excellent preparation on your part.” Ahmadi sits in silence. Amitha sits in silence. The lightbulb fails to hum. At some point, Ahmadi stands up. “Before you continue eliminating Overseer Two’s lieutenants, draft an SCP report to explain the loss of the safehouse. Part of the coverup. Blame the PENTAGRAM. Egret will bring the details. I expect nothing less than perfection. Consider it your slap on the wrist.” Ahmadi pauses in the doorway. “Congratulations on your victory, my Archmagus. Make good use of those minds. Just remember. Briar taught you everything he knew. My submind taught you everything it knew. They were not my equals.” Amitha sits in the room for several minutes after the door closes. Forget the drudgery ahead. What she’s learned from Briar and Tenchu will accelerate her research tenfold. She can’t wait to get to work. All she has to do is lie. How difficult can it be? ----- > **Item #:** SCP-9660 > > > **Object Class:** Neutralized > > > **Special Containment Procedures:** Cleanup and containment of SCP-9660’s deployment site is being handled by Mobile Task Force Alpha-1 “Red Right Hand”.  Reverse engineering of SCP-9660 is under the purview of the ECRG, led by Mathematics Chair Amitha Sanmugasundaram. Further details are restricted to Level 4/9660 as part of ongoing counter-operations. > > > **Description:** SCP-9660 was a targeted bioweapon deployed by the Pentagram, displaying numerous innovations in anomalous mathematics and biology that would have otherwise classified it as an eigenweapon if not for the highly localized nature of the tool, used to identify and assassinate key Foundation personnel responsible for counterintelligence and anti-espionage operations…

Plilt did most of the hard work on this, but ants are really, really cool and if this gets more than 25 upvotes I'm getting one tattooed on my body.

Item #: SCP-9663

Object Class: Euclid

Special Containment Procedures: A 1-kilometer radius containment zone around SCP-9663 is to be cordoned off behind a heavy-duty barbed wire fence. A single gate to this fence is to be constructed, with a gatehouse staffed by six rangers, hired by Foundation assets within South African National Parks (SANParks) as Level 0 personnel and informed that the fence protects a scientifically valuable but potentially invasive tree population. Every day, the entire perimeter of the fence is to be inspected for damage, and repairs are to be made as needed. The stationed rangers are also to monitor any new growth of SCP-9663 stems, and prune growth outside of the original extent of the anomaly.

Any individuals found within the containment zone without authorization are to be amnesticized and returned to the entrance of South Africa's Kruger National Park. Any rangers that see SCP-9663 endemics will be interviewed and amnesticized if necessary.

A segment of SCP-9663.

Description: SCP-9663 is an anomalous Vachellia erioloba (camelthorn tree), located within South Africa's Kruger National Park. Unlike other instances of this species, the anomaly takes the form of a clonal colony,1 and forms a single multi-stem tree which covers an area of at least 6.2 hectares within the park, with the appearance of a dense wood of unique individual trees.

SCP-9663's roots are capable of breaching into other worlds through an unknown mechanism. As such, the full size of the anomaly is unknown, though the earliest possible origin for the camelthorn acacia and the observed growth rate indicate a maximum size of 10,000 km2. Some sections of the colony may have been separated from the main body, making it impossible to determine its full extent. Only a small fraction of the worlds the anomaly extends to are known to the Foundation, and much of this information has been gathered from interrogations and intercepted communications of the Foundation's enemies.

SCP-9663 domatia on fresh twig, not yet colonized by SCP-9663-1.

As with other specimens of the camelthorn acacia, SCP-9663 produces swollen-thorn domatia to house mutualistic ant colonies, collectively classified as SCP-9663-1. Unlike other colonies of their species, SCP-9663-1 colonies not only defend SCP-9663 against herbivores, but also attack competing plants, pollinate the individual trees which comprise the anomaly,2 and travel far from the tree to hunt for prey.

All known SCP-9663-1 colonies display two properties not commonly found in ants associated with plants. Firstly, they are all supercolonies; in over two hundred hours of exploration into SCP-9663, ants of the same species have never been observed to fight each other. Different SCP-9663-1 species have been observed on rare occasions to go to war over resources, particularly on worlds with unusually resource-poor conditions, but such interactions are rare. SCP-9663 appears to have many different niches for ant species, limiting competition between them.

Secondly, all SCP-9663-1 instances make extensive use of tunnels that follow alongside the path of SCP-9663's roots, even otherwise arboreal species. These tunnels are capable of breaching into other worlds just as the roots of SCP-9663 are. It is unknown if this is a property of SCP-9663 or SCP-9663-1. Aside from these two properties, SCP-9663-1 species have not been observed to have any other unusual traits, and under laboratory conditions no SCP-9663-1 instances have been observed to construct such tunnels.

In addition to ants, many myrmecophiles3 are only found associated with SCP-9663 and use the tunnels to pass between worlds. Each group of species observed has been given a subcategorization under SCP-9663, categorized in Addendum 9663-2. The most commonly observed groups are mites, beetles, and threadsnakes. However, these myrmecophiles are extremely taxonomically diverse, including two species of bird, several species of killifish, an entirely endemic genus of spiders, and many extrauniversal taxa not similar to any Earthly form of life. None of these myrmecophiles have any documented anomalous traits.

The age of SCP-9663 is not known with certainty. No preserved remains of the trees or any associated organisms have been located, so radiometric dating is not possible. Rock art, dated to the 1st millenium CE and attributed to the San people, has been found in the area, including paintings depicting black clouds emerging from the trees to envelop humanoid figures holding axes, potentially representing instances of ant swarms attacking attempted tree fellers. Other paintings have been found with depictions of creatures unlike those found in any other San art, including six- and ten-limbed animals, suggesting that the San may have encountered life from other worlds which traveled through the anomaly.

The oldest historical records of the anomaly come from 1867 and were written by the Dutch botanist Ruud Abels. Abels noted the size and exact position of the anomaly, but did not realize its true nature and believed it to be nothing but an unusually dense grove of acacia. As far as the Foundation has been able to determine, no other entities or organizations have determined the true nature of the anomaly.

Initial Discovery: SCP-9663 first came to the Foundation's attention in 2011, following reports of impossibly-large swarms of ants attacking safari goers in Kruger National Park. Interviews with the guides and tourists indicated that the attacks began following an accident in which a safari jeep collided with a camelthorn tree (now identified as a part of the anomaly), felling it. According to all reports, within a few minutes of the tree's felling, large numbers of winged ants began swarming the area, biting and stinging all present. The group was able to escape by running approximately half a mile away from the anomaly, a distance at which the attacks ceased.

Initial surveys of the site established the presence of several species of ants undescribed by science, all of which were found to be traveling using tunnels constructed around and within the root system of the tree. The felled tree itself was found to have numerous swollen-thorn domatia, inhabited by three distinct undescribed species of ants. The site was quarantined and all non-Foundation parties amnesticized, and investigation of the anomaly commenced shortly thereafter.

This preliminary investigation revealed the existence of extensive tunnel systems alongside the anomaly's roots, with an average diameter of 22 cm. Initial boroscopy was unable to determine the extent of the tunnels, but did confirm the presence of anomalous mycorrhizal symbionts among the tree roots. A research team was dispatched to investigate further.

Addendum 9663-1: Structure

Currently mapped higher-order structure of SCP-9663. Note that <1% of known tunnels have been explored. Suffices and prefixes are omitted from labels.

SCP-9663 forms a higher-dimensional structure through its breaches into numerous other dimensions, exoplanets, and branes,4 alongside more esoteric forms of alternate realities, all collectively referred to as "worlds". Some of these worlds were previously known to the Foundation or other Groups of Interest (GoIs), while others were only identified during exploration of the anomaly; nonetheless, the connection to numerous known alternate worlds obviated their classification as a part of SCP-9663.

Connections between component worlds are mediated by the roots of SCP-9663, with higher-density clusters of roots developing around worlds with high concentrations of natural resources, connecting them to a greater number of other worlds. This is theorized to be an emergent structure of the anomaly, rather than an anomalous characteristic, as similar patterns have been observed in non-anomalous colonial organisms such as slime molds. Earth, despite being the presumed origin of the anomaly, has a relatively low number of connections when compared to other discovered worlds, suggesting that the anomaly is substantially more widespread elsewhere.

While conditions on worlds with SCP-9663 instances vary dramatically, no world has yet been found which does not meet the following criteria:

  • Atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration between 100 and 1000 parts per million (ppm).
  • Atmospheric nitrogen (N2) concentration between 67% and 83%.
  • Atmospheric oxygen (O2) concentration between 10% and 30%.
  • Annual rainfall between 150 and 1000 mm/year-equivalent.5
  • Average temperature between 9 °C and 22 °C.
  • Gravity between .5 and 1.5 g (4.9 and 14.7 m/s2).
  • Day length of between 6 and 36 hours.

Addendum 9663-2: Ecology
The ecological community associated with SCP-9663 is characterized by high endemicism, widespread fossorial adaptations, and multiple coexisting biota.6 While the section of the anomaly on any given world is mostly inhabited by indigenous species, an average of 30% of lifeforms do not originate from the world in question. On Earth, this percentage is smaller, at 15%; this is likely due to the anomaly originating from Earth.

Most species endemic to SCP-9663 are widely distributed across the multi-world structure of anomaly (see attached logs at the end of this addendum). There are few geographic barriers to migration and the climate is similar across all of the Wood. However, there are some exceptions. For example, annual killifish of the genus Nothobranchius (SCP-9663-2) are adapted to heavy seasonal monsoon cycles. During most of the year, their eggs are desiccated but hatch soon after temporary pools form following the rains. Floods have washed their eggs through the ant tunnels and spread them to other worlds, but many of the worlds connected to Earth through SCP-9663 do not have the same monsoon cycle as Kruger National Park. These worlds have acted as a barrier to their expansion, even to worlds with the appropriate seasonal cycles. The patterns of distribution of the SCP-9663-2 as well as certain other endemic species have allowed Foundation biogeographers to more accurately map out SCP-9663 than if the only sources of information were boroscope and snakebot logs.

Despite the presence of many non-native species, invasive events that can be attributed to SCP-9663 are few. SCP-████ and SCP-████ may be invasives that traveled to Earth using the anomaly, and many species have colonized W-EL-5A68T-SH/F/FDGH by traveling through the anomaly's tunnel system. However, in general the ability to disperse through SCP-9663 seems to make species poorer competitors. Foundation ecologists hypothesize that this is because of the well-known trade-off between generalist and specialist species. Species that range throughout much of the anomaly are hypergeneralists. They must be able to adapt to dramatically changing diel patterns, atmospheric compositions, microbiomes, and environmental toxins, among other factors. Ecological modeling indicates that single isolated populations of SCP-9663 endemics, with no outside immigration and an inability to access resources from other worlds, would quickly go extinct. In comparison, even generalists that are restricted to one world are specialized for that world.

Pollinator ants gathering nectar.

Common Name: Pollinator ant
Scientific Name: Crematogaster anthophilus
World of Origin: Earth
Notes: Feeds on flower petals, nectar, and pollen, the latter of which tends to stick to it and be transferred to other flowers. Main pollinator of SCP-9663 flowers, but often found on other species. Appears to require a wide range of species for optimal nutrition and so is highly mobile, moving between worlds as well as plants. This ensures high genetic connectivity for endemic plants.

Common Name: Camelthorn harvester ant
Scientific Name: Messor vachelliaphilus
World of Origin: Earth
Notes: Feeds almost entirely on camelthorn seeds. Nests harvest seeds from adjacent worlds, dispersing seeds between worlds. Also primary dispersal agent for other plant species of SCP-9663. Sister species to M. capensis.

Common Name: Camelthorn driver ant
Scientific Name: Myrmecsilva melanocephalus
World of Origin: Ravelwoods
Notes: Initially misidentified as a member of Dorylus. Later investigation indicated origin world is the Ravelwoods. Exceptionally large, with workers typically 5-8 cm in length. Has book lungs, like all Ravelwoods ants.7 Does not make use of swollen-thorn domatia but has subterranean nests. Tends to swarm larger herbivores that disturb their mounds.

Common Name: Lily ant
Scientific Name: Myrmecsilva liliumphilus
World of Origin: Ravelwoods
Notes: Smaller than related species. Enlarged jaws, with prominent stingers. Close mutualistic relationship with blood lily—clears open areas of competing plants and aggressively attacks animal life. Does not appear capable of distinguishing camelthorn driver ants from other members of the colony and will allow them to carry off entire broods as well as the queen.

Currently unnamed killifish species first located on Hethar.

Common Name: Annual killifish
Scientific Name: Nothobranchius sp.
World of Origin: Earth
Notes: Believed to be descended from N. orthonotus. Distributed widely across most worlds surveyed. Genetic testing indicates multiple speciation events over the past five thousand years, likely due to poor population connectivity and climatic variability. Species are visibly distinct, with different coloration in adult males. One of the best index species used to determine SCP-9663's higher-order structure.

Common Name: Extremophile mycorrhizal symbionts
Scientific Name: Gigaspora sp.
World of Origin: Earth Unknown
Notes: Several unique species of mycorrhizal fungus within the Gigaspora genus have been observed with substantially higher halide tolerance than Earth-native species, as well as unusually-high heat and cold tolerances. While provisionally classified as part of Biota Terra, recent genetic analysis indicates these species originated on worlds distant from Earth, with spores potentially being carried by ants through SCP-9663's root network. Reclassification under the new genus Pseudogigaspora is under consideration.

Common Name: Blood lily
Scientific Name: Pseudolilium formicaphilus
World of Origin: Ravelwoods
Notes: Has a symbiotic relationship with the lily ant. Grows poorly if not fertilized by the corpses of the species' prey. Bright orange flowers with scarlet speckles.

Common Name: Sheengrass
Scientific Name: Silvagramen iridescens
World of Origin: Ravelwoods
Notes: Mildly iridescent; can be distinguished from non-endemic relatives by silvery tint. Extremely tough and resistant to grazers, but the seeds are readily eaten by many granivores. Clumping habit. Common on slightly wetter worlds.

Common Name: Green-winged bee eater
Scientific Name: Merops viridoptera
World of Origin: Earth
Notes: Sister species of white-fronted bee-eater (Merops bullockoides). Reliant on cliff banks to nest, unlike SCP-9663-18-1. Less complex social structure and smaller colony size than other Merops species.

Common Name: Red-sided batwing
Scientific Name: Pseudochiroptera erythrolatus
World of Origin: W-TM-39T4R-S
Notes: Hexapodal, furred mammal-analogue believed to originate on extremely distal world from Earth. Middle two limbs modified into batlike wings also used for thermoregulation. Brightly colored. Feeds on insects. Fills same niche as green-winged bee-eater (SCP-9663-12-2); they are never found in the same world and act as a barrier to each other's colonization. Useful index species. Nests in burrows.

Common Name: Golden-throated tunneler
Scientific Name: Fossor flavigula
World of Origin: W-TM-39T4R-S
Notes: Hexapodal mammal-analogue. Elongated with a long, narrow muzzle. Patches of golden fur on throat used in breeding displays. Feeds on a variety of small vertebrate prey as well as ant larvae. Genetic analysis indicates distant relative of SCP-9663-18-1.

Exploration Log 9663-1
Collapse Log

Exploration Video Log Transcript

Date: 5/3/2011

Subject: SCP-9663

Team Lead: Dr. Enzokuhle Dlamini

Team Members: Jacob Jacobs, Miané Young

Garter-model snakebot, without attached optical fiber.

Opening Note: Initial surveys of SCP-9663 did not find proof of non-Terran species, leading to uncertainty over its exact nature. An accelerated evolutionary effect similar to SCP-1585 was initially suspected. However, genetic analysis and dissections of the camelthorn driver ant revealed that it was not related to any known organism. Dr. Dlamini suspected an extrauniversal origin for the species and organized an unmanned expedition into the tunnels. This expedition was conducted using a Garter-model snakebot remote operated vehicle, originally used by MTF Zeta-9 (“Mole Rats”).8

[BEGIN LOG]

Dlamini: Sound off.

Jacobs: Snakebot is ready to go.

Young: Sensor readings show no errors.

Dlamini: Good. Let's see what we're dealing with. Jacob, please have the snakebot enter the tunnel.

The snakebot begins to crawl into one of the larger tunnels. Communication is maintained by optical fiber. Inside, illuminated by LED, the tunnel is seen to be swarming with ants of various species. Camelthorn harvester ants and pollinator ants are both identified, as are Matabele ants, a species of specialist termite raiders widely distributed in Africa. Some small roots protrude into the tunnel. No other forms of life can be seen.

Young: I'm reading an increase in carbon dioxide levels, but it's slight. Could just be that we're in an ant tunnel.

Dlamini: It's likely. Keep an eye on the gravimeter just in case.

Several more minutes pass. The snakebot moves slowly through the ant tunnel, stopping for several minutes to observe an ant mimicking spider. After the spider enters a side tunnel, forward motion is resumed.

Young: There! Slight decrease in gravity. We are currently at 0.97 g.

Jacobs: No visual change—no portal or anything, and the soil looks similar to me. Dr. Dlamini?

Dr. Dlamini brings up the feed, rewinding thirty seconds.

Dlamini: There's nothing sudden, Jacob. But this soil looks redder than the soil from the initial footage. The transition may be gradual rather than sudden.

The snakebot continues traveling down the tunnel, gravity dropping gradually to 0.95 g. Eventually, light is seen from the end of the tunnel. Three minutes later, the snakebot emerges into a grove of SCP-9663. The camera is initially obscured by iridescent grass, but Jacobs has the snakebot rear up for a better view of its surroundings.

The SCP-9663 grove is centered within a grassy glade. The grove is small enough that the other side is easily seen from the snakebot's current position. Several hundred meters from the grove is the treeline of a dense forest. The trees are exceptionally tall and have twisting branches and trunks. The herbaceous plants have colorful leaves and many species are iridescent.

Young: If only we'd been able to get one of the better models. We could be gathering samples right now.

Dlamini: Once they see this, they'll have to give us better equipment.

Jacobs continues to pilot the snakebot, recording footage of the plant life. Insects are numerous, resembling groups native to Earth but visually distinct from all Terran species. Young notes that the humidity is higher than in Kruger, while the temperature is lower. No signs of sapient life are observed.

The snakebot is piloted into a rearing position on the edge of the grove and the camera is panned to survey the landscape in more detail, with no obscuring vegetation. Later analysis of the footage gives estimates for tree height ranging from 200 to 350 meters.9 As the camera pans back over previously surveyed areas, slight changes in the forest are visible, but the exploration team does not notice them at the time.

Jacobs: Not seeing any bird life. Not even any of the bee-eaters so far, and we saw the green-wingeds entering some of the tunnels.

Dlamini: Odd. Perhaps the grove simply isn't very hospitable to them so there aren't very many. We're not receiving audio.

Jacobs directs the snakebot back into the interior of the grove, attempting to locate additional wildlife. Additional insects are found, as are two reptiles and various SCP-9663 endemics. Like the insects, the reptiles closely resemble known groups (agamids and geckos) but are visually distinct from all known Terran species.

After half an hour, a column of camelthorn driver ants is found hunting. At Dlamini's direction, Jacobs pilots the snakebot to a safe viewing distance and observes their behavior. Captured prey is swiftly dismembered, but rather than immediately returning all food to the nest a previously unknown caste of the species sprays the more brightly-colored insects with an unknown substance. Observation continues for an hour.

Three hours after mission start, the snakebot's battery reaches 20% and it begins to be piloted back to base.

Jacobs: This is taking too long.

Dlamini: There should be more than enough battery to retrieve the snakebot. And if not, we can use the optical fiber as a tether.

Jacobs: No, I mean it's taking longer than it should. I reached this side of the grove in two minutes after the last time I passed the tunnel entrance. It's taken five to return there.

Young: The gravimeter shows the same read-outs, and if space was warping it should be showing up on diagnostics.

Jacobs: Maybe that's not what's going on, but something is off here.

Dlamini: SCP-9663's grove on Earth is Euclidean. It's possible that wherever the snakebot went isn't. Try to pilot the probe back using what battery remains. We can attempt to determine what's going on after we have our probe back.

The probe is retrieved without incident. It takes three times as long to reach the tunnel entrance as it did to reach the grove's border, but does not take longer to return to Earth once the snakebot has entered the tunnel.

[END LOG]

Closing Note: SCP-9663 was redesignated a medium-priority subject for research. Dr. Dlamini's second request for a Hognose-model snakebot was denied, but the SCP-9663 research team was permitted to modify the snakebot with additional sensors, an aspirator with five sample capsules, and a power cable.

Analysis of video data indicates the world the snakebot traveled to may be the known parallel world W-L37RK ("the Ravelwoods"), an inherently anomalous forested reality only known through captured Serpent's Hand documents and SCP-1326.

Date: 5/11/2011

Subject: SCP-9663

Team Lead: Dr. Enzokuhle Dlamini

Team Members: Jacob Jacobs, Miané Young

Opening Note: Given the improvement in the snakebot's capabilities, a follow-up expedition to the same tunnel as before was organized.

[BEGIN LOG]

Dlamini: [tensely] Be careful going in. I'm worried about some of the peripherals we attached.

Jacobs: Will do.

Young: All sensor readings within expected values, and I'm receiving no errors.

Jacobs begins to pilot the snakebot into the tunnel. He has to proceed much more slowly to avoid catching the snakebot's protruding peripherals on the walls of the tunnel. Towards the end of the tunnel, Jacobs samples some of the soil from the tunnel wall. Later analysis shows it to be a nutrient-poor red soil, with a slightly higher than normal cobalt content.

After emerging, Jacobs once again has the snakebot rear up and pan to give a 360 degree view of its surroundings. The SCP-9663 grove is the same as during the last expedition, but the glade has significantly more exposed rocks and a small creek is running through it. The foliage of the forest is darker and appears to possess a different texture, but it is difficult to make out more detail given the camera's resolution.

Jacobs: What the fuck.

Young: Temperature and humidity are both way lower than they should be.

Dlamini: How low?

Young: 10 degrees.

Dlamini: It's like teleportation, but too much of the groundcover there is the same. Only the trees and the landscape changed…

Young: I'm getting weird readings off the compass. The magnetic field here is weak, and it's shifting constantly. The new gravimeter is showing changing values too. It's so minor you wouldn't be able to feel it, but it's there.

Jacobs begins surveying the grove of SCP-9663. In addition to the plant life not changing, the animal life is broadly similar. Several previously observed species are not observed, and new species are observed, but this is likely due to chance.

Jacobs: Dr. Dlamini, what do you want me to prioritize for sampling?

Dlamini: [quietly] Four capsules left… [normal volume] Try for as many different orders as you can. One of each. No ants. We need to get a better idea of what this world is really like. We can hardly rely on the suspect data we've got now.

Jacobs: Will do.

Jacobs maneuvers the snakebot to aspirate a nearby spider, then continues exploration. While the snakebot does not leave the vicinity of the tunnel, over the next several hours two other organisms are collected—a large caterpillar feeding on sheengrass and a beetle amongst the leaf litter. However, far more unsuccessful attempts at sampling are made. Most animal are highly evasive, easily escaping the snakebot's aspirator.

Jacobs: Sorry, Doctor. The machine's just not agile enough.

Dlamini: Not your fault, Jacobs. This model was never designed for what we're doing with it. It does seem that the fauna here is faster than on Earth, though. Have the snakebot go down a different tunnel. You might have more luck on another world.

Jacobs directs the snakebot into a somewhat smaller tunnel. Unlike in the tunnel between Earth and W-L37RK, a major change in soil color is visible after approximately three meters of travel. After an additional two meters of travel, small peripheral tunnel entrances along the sides and roof of the main tunnel become visible, with an average diameter of around four millimeters. Small black ants can be seen scurrying between these entrances.

Dlamini: Those look like Lassius ants. But you'd expect the camelthorn harvesters to drive them off…

Jacobs stops driving the snakebot forward.

Jacobs: Should I try and catch one, Doctor?

Dlamini: Best to hold off for now. We can get some on the way out, if we don't find anything more interesting. Keep going, please.

Jacobs resumes driving ahead. After another five meters of tunnel, an entrance appears, with a blue sky visible through it. The snakebot emerges through it, and Jacobs again pilots it to a rearing position, capturing a 360 degree panorama of the surroundings. The glade of camelthorn trees appears to be surrounded by a forest of deciduous trees, visually similar to oaks and maples. These trees appear to be in the process of unfurling new leaves for spring. Young notes that local gravity, temperature, and humidity are all substantially higher than in W-L37RK. World later designated W-EL-4H9PC-S.

Dlamini: It looks like springtime in Europe here. Either we're back on Earth, or this world is much more similar to ours than the last.

Young: Looking at the compass now, it looks like this world has a substantially weaker magnetic field than ours, Doctor. Gravity is at exactly 1 g, though, so I suppose it's possible that's just an effect of the anomaly.

Dlamini: Very strange. Jacob, let's survey the area. Young, let me know if anything changes on the sensors.

Jacobs steers the snakebot in a widening spiral around the tunnel, carefully avoiding any potential snags to the cables. Aside from SCP-9663, the flora present all appear to be non-anomalous species native to southern France. Initially, no non-insect animals are observed, however after roughly fifteen minutes a barn swallow flies overhead. It circles the snakebot several times before landing in front of it. A mouse wearing a rough-spun tunic and what appears to be a wooden helmet is visible on its back, sitting on what appears to be a tiny saddle. At its side is a sword crafted from a nail.

Jacobs: Woah. Doctor, take a look at this!

Dlamini: What is—huh. Well, we're certainly not on Earth. Jacobs, keep the camera fixed on it, and try and give it a bit of distance. I don't want to risk it swinging that nail at our new sensors.

Jacobs: Understood, doctor.

The mouse dismounts its steed and slowly approaches the snakebot, walking on two legs and holding the nail in its right forepaw. As it approaches, Jacobs slowly backs the snakebot away, maintaining a separation of roughly one meter. After a few minutes of this, the mouse turns and runs back toward its mount, taking off once again.

Dlamini: [muttering] If only we had a Hognose, we could've tried to capture that mouse. I wonder what it could've told us. [normal volume] Resume the search. Maybe we can find something else worth bringing back.

After an additional five hours of searching, the team captured a beetle, which was found to be genetically similar to Alphitobius laevigatus, or the black fungus beetle. Following the collection of this specimen, the decision was made to collect a sample of the ants at the tunnel entrance and return. This was accomplished without incident. In later testing, it was discovered that this beetle was capable of basic problem-solving, roughly equivalent to the capabilities of a goat or sheep.

[END LOG]

Closing Note: Dr. Dlamini's third request for a Hognose-model snakebot was denied due to budgetary reasons.

Date: 6/26/2011

Subject: SCP-9663

Team Lead: Dr. Enzokuhle Dlamini

Team Members: Jacob Jacobs, Miané Young

Opening Note:

[BEGIN LOG]

Jacobs: All systems on my end are good.

Young: Same.

Dlamini: [drumming his fingers on the desk] Enter.

Jacobs pilots the snakebot into an unexplored tunnel. It is tighter than previous tunnels, and the snakebot's peripherals catch on the tunnel walls.

Jacobs: [wincing slightly] Miané, is the thermometer still working?

Young: … Looks to be.

Dlamini: Careful, Jacobs.

Jacobs: [quickly] Yes, doctor.

Jacobs continues maneuvering the snakebot, managing to avoid damaging it further, even as plastic and metal becomes increasingly common embedded into the walls of the tunnel.

Young: Carbon dioxide levels are spiking. 400 ppm… no, 450 ppm. Much higher concentration than an ant colony should produce. I'm also reading sulfur oxides. Air quality on the other side is very poor. If the scale went to 11, it would be that.10

The snakebot emerges from the tunnel into an abandoned industrial area, stretching as far as the snakebot's camera can see. The bare concrete surfaces of decaying factories have been colonized by hardier lichens and mosses. Grass and wildflowers are beginning to grow from cracks in the asphalt. However, pollution is still extensive. Smog limits visibility to approximately three kilometers. Abundant scrap metal and plastic litters the ground.

Young: Gravity is 1.1 g.

Jacobs pans the camera, examining the snakebot's surroundings. Only three stems of SCP-9663 are present, growing from some of the larger gaps in the asphalt. They are thin and sickly, with yellowed leaves. Based off observed growth rates, they are likely no older than five years of age. Clumps of sheengrass and early secessional Terran wildflowers are scattered around the stems.

Dlamini: [muttering to himself] It wasn't evacuated in an orderly fashion. No blast craters or signs of burning, so war's unlikely. Could be disease. Or an anomaly? [louder] We'll need to put the snakebot through decontamination when it gets back. Take soil samples when convenient, Jacobs.

As Jacobs continues to pan the camera, an enormous tree of unknown species comes into view, approximately two kilometers away. Its upper branches reach into the cloud layer and the sky around it is clear of haze. Unknown flying organisms can be made out as faint specks.

Jacob zooms the camera, focusing on the tree. The flying organisms cannot be identified at this distance, but they display flocking behavior. The camera can make out individual tree leaves, but only barely; their shape cannot be resolved. The wind is blowing towards the southeast and in the wake of the tree the air is pure. Several rivers descend from top of the tree to the base, frequently breaking into waterfalls.

Young: I suppose that's what did this.

The camera pans over one of the buildings near the base of the tree. An indistinct symbol is visible, taking up one of the sides of the larger buildings. As Jacobs focuses the camera, it resolves into view. It is the snake tree symbol of the Serpent's Hand. For several seconds, the research tent is quiet.

Young: The Hand isn't supposed to be capable of something like this.

Dlamini: We don't know what happened here or if the Hand even did this. It's just… graffiti. Jacobs, head closer to the tree, we need the data.

Jacobs: [uncertainly] Yes, sir.

Jacobs pilots the snakebot towards the tree. Progress is slow, with the relatively flat terrain inhibiting movement. After approximately thirty minutes, several mostly skeletonized corpses are visible, partially trapped under concrete rebar and torn scrap metal. All are cybernetically augmented and are later identified as Overseers and Foremen of the Factory. Sheengrass tussocks grow around them, where the soil is bare.

Dlamini: Harvester ants got here quickly. Those look like older tussocks. Not much lichen on the rock or asphalt… probably still too much pollution. I'm surprised the Ravelwoods plants are handling it so well.

The snakebot makes its way towards the corpses and begins inspecting them.

Dlamini: Jacobs, don't. There's rebar there, the cables could catch.

Jacobs: Doctor, this could concern a GoI. Don't we have to?

Young: Yeah.

Dlamini: Jacobs, I'm in charge of this expedition. While I'll include this in our report to regional command, I deem investigating this an unacceptable hazard to our equipment, and it's irrelevant to our task of investigating SCP-9663's ecology. Please take a soil sample and then continue to move towards the tree. We can investigate this on a later expedition if we need to; they're not going anywhere.

Jacobs: [doubtful] Yes, doctor.

Jacobs zooms the camera and briefly scans over the corpses before taking a soil sample using the aspirator. Dlamini drums his fingers somewhat impatiently, but does not comment. After taking the soil sample, Jacobs resumes his path towards the tree.

Young: The air is purer here. Air pollution levels are dropping. [glances over at the video feed] Despite us being upwind of the tree. We're in band 8.

Dlamini: Interesting. That could be an anomalous effect, or just diffusion of the pure air near the tree.

After several hours, the snakebot is halfway to the tree. Increasing quantities of rubble and scrap make it difficult for the snakebot to maneuver safely. Additional soil samples are gathered, as is one water sample. All observed organisms are SCP-9663 endemics, aside from the tree and several species of ants. Despite the distance from the SCP-9663 stems, biodiversity is much higher near the tree. Its roots have exposed large areas of soil where sheengrass and small bushes grow and species such as golden-throated tunnelers and green-winged bee-eaters are observed. Flocks of the latter were the flying organisms previously observed on camera.

While trying to examine a killifish tentatively identified as belonging to a previously identified species, Jacobs accidentally catches the power cable on a protruding piece of rebar. As he realizes his mistake, the snakebot loses its balance and falls.

Dlamini: Jacob!

Jacobs: Fucking shit!

Young: We just got a power loss!

Jacobs regains control of the snakebot before it falls into a patch of mud.11 He maneuvers to a more stable location.

Dlamini: [quickly] Jacobs, check the optical fiber.

Jacobs: [checking] It's not at imminent risk. Miané, how am I on power?

Young: [after several seconds] You should have enough to get back. If you hurry.

Dlamini: Do so. We can't risk trying to retrieve using the optical fiber.

Over the next several hours, the team takes turns piloting the snakebot and manage to reach the entry tunnel. While the snakebot loses power before reaching Earth, the team is able to use a snake hook to retrieve the snakebot.

[END LOG]

Closing Note: World designated W-EL-5A68T-SH/F/FDGH. Analysis of the soil sample after the mission was over showed high concentrations of heavy metals, many times higher than safe levels. High levels of persistent organic pollutants were also present. At the time Dr. Dlamini filed his report, W-EL-5A68T-SH/F/FDGH was not flagged for follow-up expeditions regarding the Serpent's Hand's or Factory's presence.

Dr. Dlamini noted that Technician Jacobs was not at fault for the damage to the snakebot.

Date: 7/13/2011

Subject: SCP-9663

Team Lead: Dr. Enzokuhle Dlamini

Team Members: Jacob Jacobs, Miané Young

Opening Note: After replacing several circuit boards damaged by saltwater on W-EL-9TB30,12 the SCP-9663 research team attempted a survey of an unexplored tunnel located in W-EL-5A68T-SH/F/FDGH.

[BEGIN LOG]

Jacobs: Camera and servos are good.

Young: Sensors are all working perfectly. Even the new thermal imager.

Dlamini: Excellent. Jacobs, head in.

Jacobs pilots the snakebot into the tunnel leading to W-EL-5A68T-SH/F/FDGH. While at several points peripherals catch on the sides of the tunnel, the research team has ruggedized the snakebot over the past two months. No damage is inflicted upon the snakebot, though the team grimaces at several points. Upon arriving in W-EL-5A68T-SH/F/FDGH, Jacobs briefly rears up the snakebot to pan the camera.

Dlamini: Doing better than the last time. I see new growth.

Young: A bit warmer, too. Do you think it's summer, or do you think it's the smog in the upper atmosphere clearing?

Dlamini: We should be able to find out soon.13

The snakebot is piloted into the unexplored tunnel. The soil gradually dries and becomes more reddish. No artificial materials are observed after the first hundred centimeters. Air pollution and carbon dioxide levels drop dramatically, with Young calling out lowered numbers approximately once a minute.

After ten minutes, the snakebot emerges into a grassland. The snakebot is on the edge of the SCP-9663 grove, and panning the camera back towards the grove indicates that it is one of the larger groves observed so far. Most of the grasses surrounding the grove are green, but some patches are reddish. Scattered trees are visible across the plains, with flowers in many colors. Panning the camera, golden-throated tunnelers and red-sided batwings are visible amongst the SCP-9663 grove, as well as several other species of batwing and a variety of bird-analogues.

In the distance are a herd of grazing animals. Zooming the camera reveals that they are black and white equinoid organisms, with six legs and four eyes.

Stormclouds are visible to the west. The sun is low in the sky; later spectral analysis indicates that the star is a blue giant. On the horizon is a gas giant with a prominent set of rings.

Young: Temperature is 30 degrees. Humidity is 84%. Virtually no air pollution. Air pressure is a bit on the low side, though. Either we're high elevation or this planet—

Jacob: I think it's a moon.

Young: —or this moon has a thinner atmosphere than Earth does. Gravity is the same as Earth's.

Dlamini: Something to check if we can ever get a weather balloon there. Jacobs, see if you can get any feathers from the other batwing species in the aspirator.

Jacobs moves the snakebot in a spiral around the exit point, aspirating several feathers as well as several small leaves and a soil sample. These are all kept in the same chamber. During this time, Jacobs records audiovisual data of different batwing species for later ethological analysis. The team discusses minor details regarding different species' behavior amongst themselves; for a complete transcript consult RAISA.

After completing the initial survey, Jacobs begins to pilot the snakebot out of the grove. Tall grass limits visibility, but the team is able to collect better footage of the equinoids and additional plant and insect-analogue samples.

Two hours and fifteen minutes after mission start, red fabric is briefly visible through the grass towards the southwest.

Jacobs: Thought I saw something. I'm going to try and climb to a better vantage point. Miané, can you rewind and try to figure out what that was?

Jacobs moves towards a nearby bush and starts piloting the snakebot up the trunk, careful to avoid looping the optical fiber or power cable over anything. Young reviews the footage.

Young: It looked almost like a sail.

Simplified model of vehicle. Platforms, bladders, and sails have been left out to better show gait pattern.

The snakebot reaches a meter above ground level. Jacobs pans the camera back towards the southwest, bringing what appears to be a vehicle made of a complex array of wooden rods, sails, and cloth bladders into view. The vehicle is approximately one hundred meters away and is roughly two dozen meters long and ten meters tall. The bladders alternately inflate and deflate, rapidly driving the vehicle's many legs over the terrain. Covered platforms are placed irregularly throughout the vehicle's structure. It is on a path approaching the snakebot.

Dlamini: Oh, this is amazing. [pauses] We can't approach too closely, but Young, can you try to boost the gain?

The vehicle comes to a stop as Jacobs zooms the camera in, about thirty meters away. A large spider drops from one platform near the front of the vehicle and begins inspecting the vehicle. Three hexapodal vulpinoids with reflective silver fur clamber out from a platform near the side and start harvesting the reddish grass and hunting golden-throated tunnelers. The four entities converse with each other. Later audio analysis indicates that the two species are speaking different languages, but do not appear to have any difficulties in understanding each other's speech.

Three minutes later, six smaller hexapodal vulpinoids leave the vehicle. Unlike the first three, these do not have reflective fur nor do their middle limbs end in hands, so they are believed to be a separate species. They begin running around the vehicle and playing with each other, occasionally drawing snarls from the first three vulpinoids when they interrupt the work.

One of the smaller vulpinoids approaches the bush the snakebot is on.

Jacobs: Doctor?

Dlamini: Keep still; this can't move fast enough to get away. Maybe it won't notice the probe.

After urinating on the bush, the vulpinoid spots the snakebot and begins sniffing it. The team waits to see if it leaves. It does not, jumping up to try and grab the snakebot with its teeth. While the first lunge misses, it comes dangerously close to biting down on the snakebot. The nearby sapients do not appear to notice.

Jacobs: Okay, we're going.

Jacobs drops the snakebot to the ground. While the impact jars the probe, it is still functional and the vulpinoid is startled. Jacobs begins piloting the snakebot back towards the grove.

Young: Why not head for the bush?

Jacobs: Because I'm worried it'll chew the cables.

Despite the team having previously improved the snakebot's speed, Jacobs is unable to move far enough away from the vulpinoid before it pounces. It grasps the snakebot in its jaws and begins shaking it. The camera's field of vision moves rapidly, rendering interpretation difficult.

Dlamini: Damn it!

Jacobs: [sighs] I'm going to start autoretrieval.

Young: Thermometer, humidimeter, and microphone are all throwing up error signals.

Jacobs activates the winch system and begins pulling the snakebot back by the power cable. However, retrieval speed is slower than expected, likely due to the vulpinoid bracing itself.

Jacobs: [resigned] I think it's playing tug-of-war.

Suddenly, the snakebot is dropped. The camera captures footage of the vulpinoid running back towards the vehicle before hitting the ground. The impact leaves the camera nonfunctional.

Young: And we just lost the aspirator.

Jacobs: Goddammit!

For several minutes, the team is silent. While no more data is being recorded from the probe, they do not turn off the audio recorder in the research tent.

Young: Doctor? How's our budget looking?

Dlamini: Bad. I'm sorry. The last upgrades… I've been paying out of pocket for some of the parts.14 We can probably get basic functionality back. And we can probably get a new camera and microphone. But the aspirator system…

Jacobs: Isn't the next requisition cycle coming up?

Dlamini: Yeah, but you know they're not giving us anything. We're technically researching a Euclid-class, but it's not really an active containment risk. No money for us. We're not working with a Keter-class, or something we can reverse engineer, or on something GoI-related… [trails off]

Dlamini: I know how to get us more funding.

[END LOG]

Closing Note: World designated W-TM-39T4R-S. Dr. Dlamini requested a Hognose-model snakebot for a fourth time, citing the clear Serpent's Hand presence and potential dramatic increase in their capabilities shown from Exploration Log 9663-7.

Collapse Log

On 7/15/2011, Commander John Mercer of MTF Tau-9 ("Bookworms") requested that testing be conducted on using SCP-786 in conjunction with SCP-9663 to insert teams of Tau-9 operatives into worlds with Serpent's Hand activity. This request was approved by O5-3. Given the sensitive nature of this testing, Dr. Dlamini and his team were reassigned to investigate other anomalies, with shifts in budgetary priorities being given as a cover story.15 Due to scheduling conflicts and other ongoing investigations, MTF Tau-9 was unable to begin testing until 6/15/2016.

Incident Report 9663-1
Collapse Report

On 6/18/2016, Tau-9 operatives using a prototype Mamba-model snakebot confirmed that the world Dr. Dlamini described in Exploration Log 1 was in fact W-L37RK ("The Ravelwoods"). A five-member fireteam (Fireteam Gulliver) was assembled to act as a forward scouting party into this world, and were inserted by using SCP-786 to reduce their proportions to 1/12 scale, at which size they were able to proceed through the existing tunnel single-file. To reduce the risk of attack by the ants inhabiting the tunnel, the fireteam was equipped with gas masks and the entire tunnel system around the selected entrance flooded with chloropicrin and methyl bromide.16

During their transit through the tunnel, the team voiced concern that not all of the ants had died from the fumigation, specifically mentioning that the deeper into the tunnel they passed, the greater the number of ants seemed unaffected. Earth-side Tau-9 control determined that this was likely due to a lack of airflow through the tunnel, and installed a fan over the tunnel entrance to spread the fumigant deeper; they also increased the pesticide concentration. When this still failed to achieve the desired results, one of the supervising researchers suggested pumping the gas through SCP-786 to shrink the pesticide molecules, as smaller gasses disperse faster. On-site command approved this proposal, and the anomaly was placed over the fan at the tunnel entrance.

At the same time, Fireteam Gulliver emerged from the tunnel and encountered specimens of several previously-unknown ant phenotypes.17 These specimens were universally hostile towards the fireteam, and engaged both by spraying concentrated formic acid in a manner similar to Formica archboldi, and by attempting to bite fireteam members with their mandibles. The fireteam requested backup from the Earth-side team, who removed the fan and replaced the funnel over the entrance, with the intent being to send additional Tau-9 members through to act as fire support.

Before this was possible, numerous SCP-9663-1-15 and -27 instances, no longer blocked by the fan's grate, were able to travel through SCP-786, scaling themselves up by a factor of 1218 in the process, and overrunning the Earth-side camp. While these instances eventually expired due to overheating and hypoxia,19 they remained a threat for roughly 35 minutes after enlargement. Of the eight personnel present at the camp at the time of the incursion, four were killed by the ants within the first minute.

The remaining four personnel evacuated to their nearby vehicles, which, as standard for MTF vehicles, were equipped with armor thick enough to hold the ants off indefinitely. However, in the panic this fact was forgotten, and rather than hunker down and wait for reinforcements from Foundation command, Lt. Lucius Jeffries made the decision to attempt to remove SCP-786 from the tunnel mouth and attempt to stem the tide. By this time, at least 600 enlarged instances of SCP-9663-1-15 and -27 are believed to have been present in the vicinity, along with tens of thousands of non-enlarged instances from nearby tunnels. Arming himself with incendiary grenades, spare canisters of pesticide, and a combat knife, Lt. Jeffries managed to fight his way to the entrance, where he dislodged SCP-786 from the entrance, stopping the flow of enlarged ants through the tunnel and drawing the focus of the swarm to himself.

Unfortunately, by dislodging the anomaly he allowed instances already present to travel through it again. Due to the sheer number of swarming ants in the area, thousands of individual, previously normal-sized instances became enlarged, and at least six previously-enlarged SCP-9663-1-27 instances increased their scale by another factor of 12, reaching body lengths of up to 5 meters. At this size, they presented a substantial threat to the three MTF members still inside of the vehicles. Lt. Jeffries successfully killed two of these enlarged instances with incendiary grenades before succumbing to his wounds, at which point the swarm's attention was drawn to the three remaining MTF members. While Lt. Jeffries had been attempting to stem the tide, these operatives had contacted their superiors in Tau-9, who requested close air support to bombard the swarmed area; this request was denied due to the risk of damaging SCP-9663 and/or SCP-786.

After approximately 4.5 hours, the swarm exhausted itself. Due to their vastly increased metabolic needs and size, the double-enlarged instances collapsed from apparent heat exhaustion before reaching the vehicles, and all three MTF members were recovered with only minor physical injuries. Lt. Jeffries was posthumously awarded the Foundation Cross for exceptional bravery in the line of duty. SCP-786 was recovered and returned to containment at Site 19. The radio used to communicate with Fireteam Gulliver, forgotten by the Earth-side team during the incursion, was badly damaged, but recovered black-box records indicated that the fireteam managed to fight the swarm for at least fifteen minutes, losing at least two members, before retreating into the Ravelwoods; they are considered Missing In Action with a low likelihood of survival.

Collapse Report

Following this incident, MTF Tau-9 ceased all investigation into using SCP-9663 as a method of investigating Serpent's Hand activity across alternate worlds. Exploration of W-L37RK using Mamba-model snakebots is ongoing, with the goal being the recovery of the three MIA Tau-9 operatives.
